passage: Hiroshi's exams started on Monday, and every evening that week had gone the same way: open the history textbook, hear the ping of the game's daily reward, "just check it", and look up an hour later. On Thursday he tried something different. Before sitting down, he went into the game's settings and switched off every notification. Then he carried his phone to the kitchen in their Yokohama flat and left it charging on top of the rice cooker, two rooms away. His sister Astrid raised an eyebrow. "Giving it to me?" "Just keeping it far." Back at his desk, the room was strangely quiet. He got through two chapters before he even thought about the game. When he went to fetch water, he didn't pick up the phone.

qa.q: Where did Hiroshi leave his phone?
qa.a: In the kitchen, charging on top of the rice cooker, two rooms away.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi keep 'just checking' the game earlier in the week?
qa.a: The pings of the daily reward made Hiroshi restless and curious, and in the moment a quick check always felt harmless.

qa.q: Why did Thursday's plan work better than trying harder?
qa.a: Turning off notifications and moving the phone removed the pull altogether, so he didn't need to keep resisting it.

qa.q: What might Astrid think when Hiroshi says 'Just keeping it far'?
qa.a: Astrid may be surprised and a bit impressed that her brother chose to move the phone himself rather than be told.

grounding: A teenager in Japan mutes game alerts and moves his phone to another room before revising, instead of relying on willpower.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the residential school, study hour began at seven. Shalini used to keep her phone in her lap under the desk, promising herself she wouldn't open her game. By 7:10 she always had. This term she tried a new routine. At 6:55 she muted the game's notifications and dropped her phone in the locker box outside the warden's room, where it stayed till nine. Her roommate Kavitha teased, "So dramatic. Can't you just not touch it?" "I tried 'just not touching it' for a whole year," Shalini said. That evening she finished a full chemistry chapter and the practice questions. At nine she picked up her phone, played one round, and went to bed.

qa.q: Where did Shalini put her phone during study hour?
qa.a: In the locker box outside the warden's room, where it stayed till nine.

qa.q: Why did Shalini's old promise to herself keep failing?
qa.a: With the phone in her lap, Shalini felt a constant, restless pull toward the game, and in the moment one peek always felt fine.

qa.q: What did Shalini's new routine do that willpower alone couldn't?
qa.a: Muting the game and locking the phone away changed her surroundings, so there was nothing to resist while studying.

qa.q: Why might Kavitha think 'just not touching it' should be enough?
qa.a: Kavitha may believe self-control is only about trying harder, without seeing how much having the phone close made it hard for Shalini.

grounding: In a school hostel, a teenager mutes her game and locks her phone away before study hour instead of gritting her teeth.

passage: Tarun, you asked how I got through board prep without failing chemistry. Okay, real talk. I'm Nilesh, and I used to sit at my desk with the phone face-down, telling myself, don't touch it, don't touch it. Then the clan-battle alert buzzed and it was over. Every single night. I thought I just had zero willpower. Then my cousin said, "Why are you fighting it? Move it." So at seven I'd mute every game alert, walk the phone to the kitchen and plug it in next to Dadi's radio. The kitchen's two rooms away, and Dadi asks questions if you wander in. 😅 Honestly, I still wanted to play. But wanting it from two rooms away is way easier than wanting it from ten centimetres.

qa.a: The cousin's 'Move it'; Nilesh stopped fighting the phone at the desk and changed the setup instead, muting the alerts and leaving the phone two rooms away.

qa.a: Tarun might feel less ashamed, since Nilesh admits still wanting to play, and see that a small change of place can do what gritting teeth couldn't.

passage: The night before her history test in Cape Town, Zanele knew what would happen if her phone stayed on the desk: one quick look at the game, then an hour gone. It had happened on Tuesday. Twice she reached for the empty spot where the phone usually sat. By ten she had finished two chapters. She collected the phone from the bread drawer, played one round of the game, and went to bed.

passage: At the boarding school hostel, evening study ran from seven to nine, and phones were allowed in rooms. On Monday he walked down to the warden's office at 6:55 and handed his phone over. 'You can keep it,' the warden said, surprised. 'I know,' Vishal said. 'I don't want to.' Back in the room, his roommate Omkar was already three races in, the sound up. Vishal put in earplugs and turned his chair to face the wall. His chemistry notes had never looked so interesting. By nine he had done both worksheets. When he collected his phone, he felt oddly proud, as if he'd outsmarted himself.

passage:
Dear Chetan Bhai,
You asked how I finally got through board revision without the game eating my evenings. Honestly, I gave up trying to be strong.
For months I told myself, 'Just one match, then study.' One match became six. So in January I changed the room instead of changing me. I muted every game notification. I gave my phone to Ammi at seven every evening, and she put it in her cupboard. I moved my desk away from the doorway where I could see the TV. I kept only the book I needed on the table.
The first week I kept reaching for my pocket. By the third week I didn't even think about it. My maths went from 61 to 84 in the pre-boards.
So my tip: don't fight the phone. Put it somewhere you can't reach.
Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana's maths score rise to in the pre-boards?
qa.a: It went from 61 to 84.

qa.q: What did Rehana mean by 'I gave up trying to be strong'?
qa.a: Rehana felt frustrated with willpower that kept failing and became realistic about it, so changing the room felt smarter than relying on strength.

qa.q: What changes did Rehana make to the study space?
qa.a: Muted game notifications, gave the phone to Ammi at seven, moved the desk away from the TV view, and kept only the needed book on the table.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel keeping the phone in her cupboard each evening?
qa.a: Ammi would likely feel glad to help and proud to see the maths score climb.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager explains beating a gaming habit by changing the study environment rather than relying on willpower.

Madhuri, you're sixteen and you say the game keeps pulling you from your books. Let me, your Noor Apa, tell you what I did at your age. It wasn't that long ago.
Board exams, Class 10. I had one of those racing games, and every notification was like someone calling my name. I tried everything. Promising myself. Setting timers. Guilt. Nothing lasted.
Then one evening Abbu said, “Stop fighting the phone. Just put it somewhere else.”
So I did. Notifications off, phone in the drawer in the drawing room, from six to nine. I'd walk past it and feel a twitch. But I couldn't see it, so after a while I stopped thinking about it.
I passed with a first division. Not because I became strong. Because I stopped giving myself the fight.

The chemistry board exam was the next morning, and Dilnaz's family had one room and a kitchen in the chawl. The television was on for her grandfather, the neighbours' pressure cooker whistled through the wall, and her phone kept lighting up. The squad from her racing game was online. "Final lap tonight, D!"
She had tried ignoring it for twenty minutes. Every buzz pulled her eyes back.
So she did two things. She went into the game settings and muted every notification. Then she walked to the kitchen and handed the phone to her older sister Vandana. "Keep this till ten. Even if I beg."
Vandana raised an eyebrow. "Even if you cry?"
"Especially then."
Back on the mat, the pressure cooker still whistled and the TV still blared. But the corner of her eye was quiet. She opened the chapter on acids.

qa.a: She gave it to her older sister Vandana to keep till ten.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling during the twenty minutes she tried to ignore the phone?

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Muting the notifications and handing the phone away changed her surroundings, which worked better than trying to resist each buzz by force.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Dilnaz's request?
qa.a: Vandana seems amused but supportive, happy to be the keeper and ready to hold firm even if Dilnaz begs.

I'm Gautam, and this is how I finally got through the March boards. For weeks I'd sit down to revise, phone face down on the desk, telling myself I'd be strong. Then Chetan would ping: "one match? 10 min." One match became four. Every night.
The week of Holi, with the whole colony out with water balloons and my maths a mess, I tried something different. I didn't try to be stronger. I muted the game group, put the phone in the kitchen drawer under the steel plates, and told Chetan, "I'm off till nine, we'll play Sunday."
The first evening I got up twice to check, just from habit, and the drawer felt too far to bother. By the third day I forgot the phone existed until nine. It wasn't willpower. It was the drawer.

qa.a: In the kitchen drawer under the steel plates.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel, looking back at the old way of "being strong"?
qa.a: Gautam sounds wry and a little frustrated: every night of trying to resist still turned one match into four.

qa.q: Why did the drawer work better than willpower?
